segments.text: Hey everyone, welcome back to the channel, it's me again, and I hope you're
all doing really well today.
So, um, today I felt like talking a little bit about a trip I
took a while ago, and we'll just see where this goes.
Before we get into it, a quick hello to all the new faces, and
also to everyone who has been here since the start, you know who you
are.
Here is the plan I am going to walk you through: three days in
Lisbon, excluding flights, for under three hundred euros total.
I did this trip myself last spring, tracked every euro, and I will show
you exactly where the money goes.
Day one is the old town: Alfama, the castle on the hill, and dinner
near the river.
Getting there is half the fun, and from London the flight to Lisbon takes
about forty-five minutes, so you can easily go for a long weekend.
I stayed in a hostel dorm in Alfama, booked two weeks ahead, which kept
the biggest cost of the trip down.
Breakfast was included, so always check that before you book, because it saves you
a separate cafe bill every morning.
The castle on the hill costs a few euros to enter, and the view
over the rooftops is worth every cent.
For lunch I grabbed a bifana, that classic pork sandwich, standing at a counter
with the locals for a few euros.
Trams get packed around midday, so I walked most of the old town, which
cost nothing and was honestly the best part.
Speaking of walking, this reminds me of this orange street cat that followed me
all the way from the cathedral down to the river.
He had one torn ear and he walked like he owned the place, stopping
every few steps to check that I was still behind him.
I named him Captain, bought him a sardine from a grill stand, and he
ate it in about four seconds flat.
I still think about Captain whenever I see an orange cat, which has nothing
to do with budgets, but there it is.
Okay, back to the money.
Day two was the museums and the tower out at Belem, plus the famous
custard tarts nearby.
A pastel de nata costs about a euro fifty in most Lisbon bakeries, so
I gave myself two a day as my little luxury.
Day two total: forty-five for the bed, twenty for food, ten for transport, so
seventy-five for the day.
Let me add that up again slowly so you can follow: forty-five for the
hostel, plus twenty for food, that makes sixty-five.
Sixty-five, plus ten for transport, that is seventy-five for the day.
Seventy-five.
And just to double-check: forty-five plus twenty is sixty-five, plus ten is seventy-five.
Yes, seventy-five a day.
So over three days, seventy-five times three is two hundred and twenty-five, which leaves
room for one nice dinner.
Day three was free: the viewpoint at Graca in the morning, the market hall
at lunch, and a slow evening by the water.
All in, I spent just under my target, and I never felt like I
was missing out on anything.
That works out to about ninety dollars a day, which is less than a
single night out in Austin, Texas, if you think about it.
And if you split a room with friends, just have everyone send their share
over Zelle on the last night, easy.
So that's the whole trip: the old town, Belem, and one slow day, all
under three hundred euros.
Try it yourself, track every euro like I did, and you will be surprised
how far the money goes.
And that's my trip.
Thanks for watching, bye.
